title: Finite modules over a matrix algebra over a division algebra
statement: Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $D$ be a finite-dimensional division $K$-algebra, and let $d\geq1$. Here division means a nonzero unital ring in which every nonzero element is invertible, with a unital homomorphism $K\to Z(D)$. Put $B=M_d(D)$ [def-weil-matrix], with row-column multiplication, and let $S=D^d$ be its column module. A left $B$-module is understood to have the induced compatible $K$-vector-space structure. Then $S$ is simple [def-weil-pbc-simple-module], every finite-dimensional left $B$-module is isomorphic to $S^{\oplus n}$ for a unique integer $n\geq0$, and every simple left $B$-module is isomorphic to $S$. Finally, right multiplication in every coordinate induces a $K$-algebra isomorphism $$D^{\mathrm{op}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{End}_B(S),\qquad a^{\mathrm{op}}\longmapsto((v_j)_j\mapsto(v_ja)_j).$$ Here $D^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same addition as $D$ and reversed multiplication; $\operatorname{End}_B(S)$ consists of additive $B$-linear maps with composition as multiplication.

proof.text: Let $N$ be finite-dimensional over $K$ and set $V=eN$. The left $D$-action on $V$ is $a\cdot v=(aI_d)v=E_{11}(a)v$, the equality following from $ev=v$. For a finite $K$-basis $(x_t)$ of $N$, the vectors $(ex_t)$ span $V$ over $K$, since $e(\sum_t c_tx_t)=\sum_t c_t ex_t$. They therefore also span over $D$: the given central structural map $K\to D$ realizes each $K$-coefficient as a $D$-coefficient. Apply [lem-per-division-ring-finite-basis] to obtain a finite left $D$-basis $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ of $V$. This includes $N=0$, for which $n=0$.

source.place: Tag 074E, lemma-simple-module-unique, proof of (2), finite free module over the skew field.

proof.text: Apply [lem-per-matrix-corner-reconstruction] with $R=D$ to get $N\cong V^d$. If $v_i=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_t$, send $(v_i)_{i=1}^d$ to the $n$ columns $((a_{it})_{i=1}^d)_{t=1}^n$. Uniqueness of basis coordinates gives an additive bijection $V^d\cong S^{\oplus n}$. It is $B$-linear because the coefficient of $b_t$ in $\sum_j A_{ij}v_j$ is $\sum_j A_{ij}a_{jt}$, precisely the $i$th coordinate of $A$ applied to column $t$. This proves existence of the required decomposition.

proof.text: If $S^{\oplus n}\cong S^{\oplus m}$ as $B$-modules, restrict the isomorphism and its inverse to the image of $e$. Both commute with $e$ and with $aI_d$ for $a\in D$, so this gives a left $D$-linear isomorphism $D^n\cong D^m$, by taking the first entry in each column. Transporting the standard basis of $D^n$ along this map gives a basis of $D^m$ with $n$ elements. The uniqueness assertion of [lem-per-division-ring-finite-basis], compared with the standard $m$-element basis, gives $n=m$.

source.place: Tag 074E, lemma-simple-module-unique (3), uniqueness of free rank after passage to the corner.

proof.text: Let $T$ be any simple left $B$-module, without a finiteness assumption. For $0\ne x\in T$, $Bx$ is a nonzero submodule, hence equals $T$ by [def-weil-pbc-simple-module]. Fix a finite $K$-basis $c_1,\ldots,c_h$ of $D$. The finitely many vectors $E_{ij}(c_t)x$ span $T$ over $K$, since the matrices $E_{ij}(c_t)$ span $B$ over $K$. Thus the preceding decomposition applies: $T\cong S^{\oplus n}$. Nonzeroness forces $n>0$, and if $n>1$ one summand is a nonzero proper submodule. Consequently $n=1$ and $T\cong S$.

source.place: Tag 074E, lemma-simple-module-unique (1),(4); finite generation of a simple module made explicit.

proof.text: For $a\in D$, coordinatewise right multiplication $R_a(v)=va$ is additive and $B$-linear: $(Av)a=A(va)$ by associativity and distributivity. Conversely, if $f\in\operatorname{End}_B(S)$, then $f(u_1)=ef(u_1)=u_1a$ for a unique $a\in D$. Since $v=\sum_i E_{i1}(v_i)u_1$, linearity gives $f(v)=\sum_i E_{i1}(v_i)u_1a=va$. Hence $a\mapsto R_a$ is bijective, with $a$ recovered as the first entry of $f(u_1)$. It preserves addition and identity, and $R_a\circ R_b=R_{ba}$; this is precisely multiplication in $D^{\mathrm{op}}$. For $c\in K$, centrality gives $R_{c1_D}(v)=cv$, so the bijection preserves the $K$-algebra structure. This proves the specified isomorphism.
